title: MAGS: Machine-checked guarantees on specified safety properties in AI code
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 16 Sep 2026]
Title:MAGS: Multi-agent Auto-formalization Guarantees Safety for Agentic Outputs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:LLM coding agents now generate complex programs at a scale that makes thorough human review increasingly difficult, raising the risk of safety and security failures. Common approaches, including fuzz testing, static analysis, and LLM-as-a-Verifier, can detect many failures but struggle to cover all possible edge cases. Formal verification addresses this by providing machine-checkable guarantees over specified properties, but traditionally demands substantial manual specification and proof engineering. We introduce a unified multi-agent framework, MAGS, that generates executable programs with formal safety guarantees, using Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation where safety properties can be mechanically checked. MAGS formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, translates generated code into Dafny, repairs violations using verifier feedback, and compiles verified programs back into executable code. We evaluate MAGS on 100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, and 20 robotic-arm tasks. Across all 220 examples, it achieves a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against frozen specifications. Independent safety and functional evaluations further show strong performance across all three domains, while revealing failures when the auto-formalized semantics do not fully capture the target behavior.

report.summary: MAGS uses multi-agent auto-formalization and Dafny verification to produce executable code with machine-checked safety guarantees, succeeding on 220 CUDA, shell, and robotics tasks.
report.background: LLM coding agents can now generate large, complex programs faster than humans can thoroughly review them, increasing the risk of safety and security defects. Conventional safeguards—fuzz testing, static analysis, and LLM-as-a-verifier—catch many problems but cannot exhaustively cover edge cases. Formal verification can provide machine-checkable guarantees, yet it has traditionally required extensive manual specification and proof engineering. MAGS addresses this gap by combining multi-agent automation with Dafny, a verification-aware intermediate representation. It freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, translates generated code into Dafny, uses verifier feedback to repair violations, and compiles verified programs back to executable code. The work reflects a broader push to make agentic coding trustworthy in high-stakes domains such as GPU kernels, system scripts, and robotics.
key_points: MAGS treats human-audited APIs and safety requirements as frozen specifications. Generated code is translated into Dafny, checked mechanically, repaired using verifier feedback, then compiled back into executable form. This keeps the safety contract fixed while the multi-agent system iterates on implementation details.

The authors evaluate MAGS on 220 tasks: 100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, and 20 robotic-arm tasks. It reports a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against the frozen specifications, showing the approach can work across very different code domains.

Independent safety and functional evaluations found strong performance in all three domains, but the paper also reports failures when automatically formalized semantics did not fully capture the target behavior. That caveat matters: machine-checked guarantees are only as strong as the formal specification and its fidelity to real-world intent.

MAGS aims to reduce the manual burden of formal verification by using multiple agents to auto-formalize requirements and repair code. It does not prove arbitrary correctness; it checks specified safety properties. The approach is therefore best seen as a specification-anchored safety layer for agentic code generation.
report.impact: MAGS points toward a practical safety layer for agentic coding: instead of relying only on probabilistic testing or LLM reviewers, teams can attach machine-checked guarantees to high-risk generated code. For the AI industry, this could accelerate adoption in GPUs, infrastructure scripts, and robotics, where silent failures are costly. Developers may need to write or curate formal safety specifications and work with verification-aware intermediate languages, adding upfront effort but reducing downstream review. Regular users could benefit from safer generated software, but not absolute correctness: guarantees cover only frozen properties, and specification gaps remain a real risk. The paper's caveat about semantic mismatch is therefore as important as its 100% success rate.
report.tools: Watch Dafny, the open-source verification-aware language and verifier used as MAGS's intermediate representation, and the MAGS framework itself if the authors release code. Complementary tools include fuzzers, static analyzers, and LLM-as-a-verifier systems, which can catch issues outside formal specifications. For CUDA and robotics, look for verified-kernel and safety-spec formalization projects that build on Dafny-style workflows.
